title: Why Jesus Started With the Churches
paragraphs:
Why Jesus Started With the Churches
The Warning We Keep Missing—and the Grace That Still Calls Our Name
Imagine standing before the throne of God believing the greatest problem in the world is out there somewhere.
Then Jesus opens His mouth, and instead of beginning with the nations, He begins with His own people.
Instead of addressing Rome, He addresses the churches.
Instead of confronting pagan temples, He confronts congregations.
Instead of starting with the lost, He starts with those who claim to know Him.
That should stop every one of us in our tracks.

The book of Revelation is often approached as a roadmap of future events, prophetic mysteries, beasts, judgments, and end-time signs. Yet before the seals are opened, before the trumpets sound, before the bowls of wrath are poured out, before the final victory is revealed, Jesus does something unexpected.
The risen Christ begins with His own house.
The Apostle John records the vision in Revelation 1:13:
“and in the midst of the seven lampstands one like a son of man.”
The phrase “Son of Man” echoes the Aramaic language of Daniel 7:13:
This is not merely a title.
The One to whom all authority has been given.
The lampstands are identified in Revelation 1:20:
“The seven lampstands are the seven churches.”
Jesus is not distant from His church.
The Greek word repeatedly used throughout Revelation chapters 2 and 3 is “οἶδα” (oida).
The terrifying reality is that Jesus sees us more clearly than we see ourselves.
Many believers spend their lives comparing themselves to others.
But Jesus never compares us to others.
The church in Ephesus was doctrinally sound.
Many modern Christians would celebrate them as a model church.
“But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.” (Revelation 2:4)
The Greek word for love here is “ἀγάπη” (agapē).
Imagine hearing those words from Jesus.
You are doing all the right things.
Yet your heart is no longer captivated by Christ Himself.
But you no longer delight in Him.
How many believers today are living in Ephesus without realizing it?
The church in Sardis received an even more shocking diagnosis.
“You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” (Revelation 3:1)
People assumed God was moving among them.
Yet Jesus saw a spiritual graveyard behind the polished image.
How many people scrolling through social media today know exactly what that feels like?
The church in Laodicea perhaps receives the most famous rebuke.
“Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.” (Revelation 3:16)
The tragedy is not that Laodicea thought they were failing.
The tragedy is that they thought they were succeeding.
“For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,’ not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.” (Revelation 3:17)
To think we are thriving while heaven sees us starving.
To think we are rich while heaven sees us bankrupt.
To think we are clothed while heaven sees us exposed.
To think we are healthy while heaven sees us dying.
This is why Jesus starts with the churches.
Because judgment begins with the household of God.
Because the greatest threat to Christianity has never been persecution from outside.
It has always been compromise from within.
Yet what makes these letters so breathtaking is that they are not merely warnings.
Jesus does not expose sin to destroy people.
He exposes sin to rescue them.
Even in Laodicea, after delivering one of the strongest rebukes in Scripture, Jesus says:
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” (Revelation 3:20)
The Greek word “ἕστηκα” (hestēka) means He stands and remains standing.
The Savior who sees every failure is the same Savior who died for every failure.
The One who exposes our wounds is the One who still bears scars in His hands.
The One who calls us to repentance is the One who already paid the price for our redemption.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is why our theme is not scandal alone.
It is scandal transformed by grace.
The woman caught in adultery stood condemned.
The thief on the cross had wasted his entire life.
And perhaps today, you feel like your story is too broken.
But Revelation reminds us that the same Jesus who rebukes also redeems.
The same Jesus who confronts also restores.
The same Jesus who corrects also heals.
The same Jesus who starts with the churches does so because He loves them.
The Hebrew word often used throughout the Old Testament for covenant love is “חֶסֶד” (chesed).
The kind of love that refuses to quit.
The kind of love revealed perfectly at Calvary.
The kind of love that reaches into scandals and creates testimonies.
The kind of love that takes broken people and turns them into living evidence of God's mercy.
Maybe that is why Jesus started with the churches.
Not because He had abandoned them.
Not because He wanted to condemn them.
But because He wanted to restore them.
Not because He was finished with them.
And perhaps today He is knocking on your heart again.
Did this expose something hidden in your heart?
Your testimony may be exactly what another struggling believer needs to see today.
If this ministry has blessed you, supporting it is one practical way to help spread biblical truth to more people.
The same Jesus who walks among the lampstands is still walking among us tonight.
